modules.title: Data Structures & Algorithms
modules.description: The core toolkit of problem solving: how dynamic arrays grow, how to reason about cost with Big O, fast search on sorted data, and the two canonical sorting algorithms.

concepts.title: Dynamic Arrays (std::vector)
concepts.description: How std::vector works under the hood: contiguous memory, size vs capacity, doubling growth, amortized O(1) push_back, and iterator invalidation. Includes building a mini dynamic array by hand.

content.title: The problem it solves
content.content:
You need to store data whose size you don't know ahead of time: lines from a file, network packets, user clicks, sensor readings. In C, an array's size is fixed at creation: `int scores[10]` cannot hold 11 scores, and there is no way to ask the compiler to change that later. The manual workaround — allocate a bigger array and copy everything over — is exactly where memory leaks, dangling pointers, and off-by-one bugs are born.

`std::vector` solves this. It is an array that grows itself, safely, behind a tiny API (`push_back`, `size`, `operator[]`), while keeping its elements in *contiguous memory* so that underneath it is still a real, cache-friendly array. It is the single most used container in C++ production code for a reason.

content.title: Mental model
content.content:
A vector owns a block of memory with room for some number of elements — that is its *capacity*. Only the elements you have actually stored count — that is its *size*. As you `push_back`, the size grows toward the capacity. When size would exceed capacity, the vector rents a bigger block (typically twice as big), copies every element over, and returns the old block to the system.

Think of a moving company: you start in a small apartment, and when you run out of rooms you move to a place with *double* the rooms. Moving is expensive, but because each move doubles your space, you move only a handful of times no matter how many boxes you eventually store.

content.title: Simple example
Why it works: contiguous memory plus a growth strategy
content.content:
A vector holds three pieces of data: a pointer to a heap block, a `size` counter, and a `capacity` counter. Element access `v[i]` is literally `ptr[i]` — the same indexing the hardware gives you for a raw C array, so `operator[]` costs one pointer add, and a range-for over a vector is just a tight loop over contiguous addresses. That contiguity is what the CPU's cache loves: the first access pulls a whole run of elements into L1 cache, which is why iterating a vector is dramatically faster than iterating a node-based linked list on modern hardware.

`push_back` normally does `ptr[size] = x; ++size;` — O(1). Only when `size == capacity` does it perform a growth step: allocate a new block, copy every element, free the old block, update the pointer.

content.title: Amortized analysis: why doubling makes push_back cheap
content.content:
Amortized means *averaged over a whole sequence of operations*, not per-operation. Start with capacity 1 and double on every growth. Pushing `n` elements triggers copy events of size 1, 2, 4, 8, ... up to the final growth — a geometric series that sums to less than `2n` total element copies. So `n` pushes together cost O(n) copies, about 2 per element on average: most pushes are a single write, and the rare expensive growth is paid for out of the budget saved by all the cheap pushes before it. That is what "push_back is amortized O(1)" means.

Now imagine growing by exactly +1 instead: the copies are 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = O(n^2) — quadratic, unusable at scale. The growth factor is the entire difference between a container you trust and a trap.

content.title: Common mistakes
content.content:
1. **Reading or writing past size with `[]`.** `v[5]` on a vector of 5 elements is undefined behavior — `operator[]` is unchecked by design for speed. `v.at(5)` throws; `[]` doesn't. Sanitizers (ASan) catch it in tests; in production it silently corrupts memory.

2. **Keeping a reference across growth.** `int& r = v[0]; v.push_back(x);` — if that push triggers reallocation, `r` dangles and reading it is UB. Reallocation invalidates *every* iterator, pointer, and reference into the vector.

3. **Signed/unsigned comparisons.** `for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)` compares `int` with `size_t`. It usually works, and then fails in the sneakiest ways (e.g. `v.size() - 1` on an empty vector is a huge unsigned number, not -1). Cast explicitly: `(int)v.size()`.

4. **Forgetting that growth copies elements.** Storing heavy objects in a vector and pushing a million times re-copies objects during every growth event. Use `reserve()` when you know the final size, or move/emplace to avoid copies.

content.title: Real-world use
content.content: The doubling dynamic-array strategy is everywhere: Python's `list`, JavaScript's arrays, Go slices, and Rust's `Vec` all use exactly this pattern. Game engines store vertices, textures, and entity lists in dynamic arrays because contiguous layout feeds the GPU and the CPU cache pipeline. Databases use dynamic arrays for columnar table storage and for in-memory intermediate results. When you see `reserve()` + `push_back` loops in production C++, this is what the author was tuning: eliminating growth events so the amortized cost never becomes visible.

content.title: When NOT to use it
content.content:
A dynamic array is a sharp tool, not a universal one:

- **Frequent insertion at the front or middle** — every insert shifts all following elements, O(n). Prefer `std::deque` for front work or `std::list` when you need splicing.
- **You need stable addresses.** Any reallocation moves every element; if other code holds pointers into the container (a graph keeping `Node*`s), a vector silently invalidates them. Index-based storage survives growth.
- **Fixed, compile-time-known size** — that is what `std::array` is for.
- **Guaranteed worst-case latency.** Amortized O(1) means *average*; a single `push_back` can still cost O(n) when it triggers growth. Real-time audio or control loops cannot stall for a reallocation.
- **Huge elements pushed often** — each growth copies everything; reserve ahead or store by move/emplace.

content.title: Iterator and reference invalidation rules
content.content:
The rules matter more than the details, because violating them is UB you won't see until a production crash:

- `push_back`/`insert`/`resize` that triggers **reallocation** invalidates all iterators, pointers, and references.
- `push_back` that does *not* reallocate invalidates only the past-the-end iterator.
- `erase` invalidates iterators at and after the erased position.
- **Never keep an iterator across a modifying call.** This is why `for (int x : v) v.push_back(y);` crashes — the range-for holds an iterator that the push invalidated. If you must modify while iterating, iterate by index or build a new vector.

content.title: What you just learned
content.content:
- A vector is a dynamic array: `size` live elements inside a `capacity`-sized contiguous heap block.
- Contiguity gives O(1) indexing and cache-friendly iteration; that is why it beats linked lists in practice.
- Growth is geometric (typically 2x), which makes `push_back` amortized O(1): n pushes cost about 2n copies total.
- Growth by +1 would be O(n^2) — the growth factor is the whole game.
- Reallocation invalidates every iterator/pointer/reference; never hold them across mutating calls.

exercises.title: Mini dynamic array: grow as you push
exercises.promptMd: Implement `buildFromPush(int n)` — a miniature std::vector. Use raw `new[]`/`delete[]` and manually double the capacity whenever the array is full, exactly like vector's growth strategy. Push the values 0, 1, ..., n-1 and return the final contents as a `std::vector<int>`. Your code must not leak memory: the raw heap buffer is freed before returning.

hints.text: Track three locals: `int* data`, `int size`, `int capacity`. The value pushed at step i is i.
When `size == capacity`, allocate a new block of `(capacity == 0 ? 1 : capacity * 2)`, copy the old `size` elements over, then `delete[]` the old block before pointing `data` at the new one.
After the loop, build the result with `std::vector<int> result(data, data + size);` then `delete[] data;` — handle n == 0 (data stays nullptr; the range is empty).

exercises.explanationMd: This is the exact growth loop std::vector runs: push in O(1) until full, then allocate double, copy, and free the old block. The geometric growth keeps the total copy cost at O(n) across all n pushes. Note the `(capacity == 0) ? 1 : capacity * 2` starting point, and that the raw buffer is freed before returning — otherwise you leak memory. Building a `std::vector` from the raw buffer makes the return value work with the harness (returnType vector<int>, comparator array).

exercises.title: Count the copies in doubling growth
exercises.promptMd: Implement `countGrowthCopies(int n)` — the total number of element copies that happen while pushing values 0, 1, ..., n-1 into a dynamic array that starts at capacity 0 and **doubles** when full (first growth brings capacity to 1). Count only copies performed inside growth events. Return the total as `long long`. For n = 4 the copy events are sizes 0, 1, and 2, so the answer is 3.

hints.text: Simulate only the growth events: a growth happens exactly when the next 0-based index being pushed equals the current capacity.
When you grow from capacity c to 2c you copy c existing elements — add c to the total, then double capacity (or set it to 1 on the first growth).
For n = 5, growth events are at indices 0 (copy 0), 1 (copy 1), 2 (copy 2), 4 (copy 4) — total 7. Return `long long` so large n can't overflow.

testCases.description: copy of 1 element at second push

exercises.explanationMd: Each growth event from capacity c to 2c copies the c elements already stored. The total for n pushes is 0 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... which stays below 2n — that geometric bound is precisely why push_back is amortized O(1). If the array grew by +1 instead, this function would return ~n^2/2 and the total cost would be quadratic. The edge cases: n = 0 gives 0, n = 1 gives 0 (no copies needed for one element).

exercises.title: Total cost of n push_backs
exercises.promptMd: You push n elements into an empty std::vector one at a time, and the vector uses the doubling strategy. What is the *total* cost of all n push_back calls, counting the element copies performed during growth?

hints.text: How many elements are copied at each growth event: 0, then 1, then 2, then 4, ...
Sum the geometric series 0 + 1 + 2 + 4 + ... up to the final growth and compare it to n.

exercises.explanationMd: The copies form a geometric series that sums to less than 2n, so the total is O(n) — about 2 copies per element on average. That is exactly what 'amortized O(1) push_back' means.

options: O(n log n) total, because each element may be copied at every level
O(n^2) total, because copying during growth is expensive
O(n) total, because the geometric series of copies sums to less than 2n
O(log n) total, because growth is rare

exercises.title: Trace the growth events
exercises.promptMd: A dynamic array starts with capacity 0 and doubles when full. We push the values 0 through 15 (16 pushes total). How many times does the array reallocate, and at which pushes do the reallocations happen?

hints.text: List the capacities after each growth: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. When does each growth trigger?
A growth triggers when the next 0-based index to fill equals the current capacity: pushes of indices 0, 1, 2, 4, 8.

exercises.explanationMd: Growth happens when size == capacity: after pushing index 0 (0 -> 1), index 1 (1 -> 2), index 2 (2 -> 4), index 4 (4 -> 8), and index 8 (8 -> 16). That is 5 reallocations for 16 pushes — log2(16) + 1 — which is why the average cost per push stays constant.

questions.prompt: What is the amortized time complexity of push_back on std::vector with the doubling strategy?
options: O(n) amortized, each push copies all elements
O(1) amortized, because n pushes cost O(n) total: the geometric copy series sums to under 2n
O(log n) amortized
O(1) worst case per push
questions.explanation: n pushes trigger geometric copy events (1+2+4+... < 2n), so the average cost per push is O(1). The worst case for a single push is still O(n) when it triggers reallocation.

questions.prompt: A push_back triggers a reallocation. Which of the following is now invalid to use?
options: Only iterators obtained before the push
All iterators, pointers, and references to elements obtained before the push
Only the size() value
Nothing — push_back never invalidates anything
questions.explanation: Reallocation moves every element to a new block, so all iterators, pointers, and references into the vector dangle. Only indices remain valid.

questions.prompt: What would happen if a dynamic array grew by exactly +1 instead of doubling?
options: Nothing changes; both strategies are O(1) amortized
+1 growth is O(log n) amortized
+1 growth makes n pushes cost O(n^2) total because copies are 1+2+...+n
+1 growth is faster because it wastes less memory
questions.explanation: Growth by +1 re-copies all existing elements at every step: 1+2+...+n = O(n^2). Doubling makes the copies a geometric series summing to O(n). The growth factor is the entire algorithm.

questions.prompt: Which statement about vector's contiguous memory is TRUE?
options: Contiguity makes element access O(n)
Contiguity gives O(1) indexing and cache-friendly iteration because elements sit in adjacent addresses
Vector stores elements in a linked list internally
Contiguity only matters on 32-bit platforms
questions.explanation: v[i] is ptr[i] on a single heap block, so indexing is O(1) and the CPU cache loads whole runs of elements — the main reason vectors outpace linked lists in practice.

questions.prompt: Explain why pushing n elements into an empty vector costs only about 2n element copies total, even though a single push can cost O(n). What does 'amortized O(1)' mean here, and how would the answer change if growth were +1 instead of doubling?
questions.explanation: Each growth event copies all elements currently stored. With doubling, those copy sizes are 1, 2, 4, 8, ... — a geometric series bounded by 2n. So although one push occasionally does O(n) work, that cost is spread over all the O(1) pushes that preceded it: the average over a sequence is constant, which is exactly what 'amortized O(1)' means. With +1 growth the copy sizes are 1, 2, 3, ..., n, summing to O(n^2).

concepts.title: Big O: Reasoning About Cost
concepts.description: Why complexity analysis matters, the common complexity classes, how to measure cost empirically, and what amortized analysis really means. Mostly conceptual and tracing work — no harness required.

lesson.title: Big O Notation: How Work Grows

content.title: The problem it solves
content.content:
Two programs finish in 0.1 seconds on your machine. Which is better? Wall-clock time answers that for *one* input size on *one* machine — but it says nothing about what happens when the input grows 10x, 1000x, or when the data no longer fits on one machine.

Complexity analysis is the language engineers use to answer: *how does the amount of work grow as the input grows?* It predicts failures before they exist. An O(n^2) algorithm on 10 million records takes about 100 seconds; on 100 million it takes 10,000 seconds (about 2.7 hours). Same code, same machine, just more data — and complexity analysis told you this would happen before you ever ran it.

content.title: Mental model
content.content:
Big O describes the *shape* of the growth curve, not the exact cost. Use the doubling test: double the input and watch what happens to the work.

- Work stays flat -> O(1) (constant)
- Work doubles -> O(n) (linear)
- Work quadruples -> O(n^2) (quadratic)
- Work grows by a fixed addition -> O(log n) (logarithmic)

A phone book is the classic logarithmic intuition: each look-up step throws away half the remaining pages, and you add only one step for every doubling of pages.

content.title: Simple example
Why it works: the formal definition
content.content:
`f(n)` is `O(g(n))` if there exist constants `c` and `n0` such that `f(n) <= c * g(n)` for all `n >= n0`. Two consequences fall straight out of that definition:

1. **Constants don't matter asymptotically.** `3n^2 + 40n + 9` is O(n^2) because for large n the quadratic term outruns everything else.
2. **Big O is about *eventually*.** An O(n) algorithm can be slower than an O(n^2) one on tiny inputs; what Big O promises is that once n passes some crossover point, it stays behind forever.

This is also why serious engineers both analyze and measure: analysis gives the growth curve for all machines and all scales; measurement gives today's constants on today's hardware.

content.title: The common complexity classes
content.content:
| Class | Name | Doubling input | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| O(1) | constant | flat | array index, hash-table lookup |
| O(log n) | logarithmic | + fixed amount | binary search, balanced tree ops |
| O(n) | linear | doubles | single pass over the data |
| O(n log n) | linearithmic | slightly more than double | merge sort, most good sorts |
| O(n^2) | quadratic | quadruples | nested loops over the data |
| O(2^n) | exponential | squares | brute-force subset enumeration |

Most production systems live in the O(n log n) band or below. Quadratic code survives only with small or hard-bounded inputs. Exponential is a loud alarm: it means the approach itself cannot scale.

content.title: Common mistakes
content.content:
1. **Writing `O(2n)` or `O(n + 5)`.** Both are O(n) — constants are dropped by definition. Say O(n), and keep the constant in your head when inputs are small.

2. **"Nested loop means O(n^2)."** Only if both loops range over the input. A loop that halves n each step (binary search) is O(log n). You count the *work per step times the number of steps*, not the braces.

3. **Confusing best, average, and worst case.** Big O conventionally means worst case unless stated. Linear search finding the target first is a lucky case, not O(1).

4. **Using Big O to declare a small problem unsolvable.** An O(n^2) sort on n = 20 can beat any O(n log n) sort because of constant factors — asymptotic claims are about large n. Conversely, don't ship an O(n^2) scan on the hot path of a request handler that serves millions of requests.

content.title: Measurement: timing and profiling
content.content:
Analysis predicts; measurement confirms. To measure honestly: run at several input sizes with `std::chrono::high_resolution_clock`, take the median of several runs, warm up the cache, and beware the optimizer deleting your entire benchmark because the result is unused (use a volatile sink or print the result).

Plot time against n on a log-log scale: a polynomial `n^k` becomes a straight line with slope `k` — slope 1 is linear, slope 2 is quadratic, slope 1.2 is something like n log n. A surprising finding: real measurements are full of cache and memory-hierarchy effects, so small-n numbers lie; only the asymptotic curve survives scale. That is why complexity and measurement are complementary, not rivals.

content.title: Real-world use
content.content: Database query planners estimate the cost of alternative execution plans using complexity models *before* running any of them — the O(n^2) join loses to the O(n log n) one without a single row being touched. Search engines size their indexes with growth models. The C++ standard library publishes complexity as a contract (`std::sort` is O(n log n), `unordered_map::find` is average O(1)), and engineers pick data structures by those contracts. And when a startup's API gets 100x traffic, the O(n^2) endpoint that was fine in the prototype is the first thing to fall over — complexity analysis is how you see that fall coming.

content.title: When NOT to use it
content.content:
- **n is small and fixed.** Constant factors dominate; a hand-tuned O(n^2) can beat a clever O(n log n) at n = 8.
- **Worst-case latency is the requirement.** Amortized O(1) (vector push_back) and expected O(1) (hash tables) still have rare expensive operations; real-time systems need worst-case guarantees.
- **Average case matters more.** Quicksort is O(n^2) worst case yet O(n log n) typical — which is why libraries use it. Always ask which bound the question cares about.
- **Memory or constant factors dominate.** An O(n log n) sort using O(n) extra space may lose to an in-place O(n^2) sort when memory is the constraint.

Big O is a tool for choosing between approaches at scale, not a verdict on micro-differences.

content.title: What you just learned
content.content:
- Big O describes how work grows with input size, independent of machine and constants.
- The doubling test gives an instant feel: flat = O(1), double = O(n), quadruple = O(n^2), +1 step = O(log n).
- Common classes: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n) — and where each lives.
- Measurement gives constants, analysis gives the curve; do both.
- Amortized and expected bounds are different from worst-case bounds — know which one you're looking at.

exercises.title: Classify the algorithms
exercises.promptMd:
Match each operation to its complexity class:
1. Accessing `v[5]` on a std::vector.
2. Finding a value in an *unsorted* array with a loop.
3. Binary search on a sorted array of size n.
4. Checking every pair of elements in an array of size n.

Which answer correctly lists classes for 1, 2, 3, 4 in order?

hints.text: v[i] on a vector is a pointer dereference plus offset — it does not scan.
A pair-check is a nested loop: n choices times n choices.

exercises.explanationMd: Vector indexing is O(1) (pointer arithmetic on a contiguous block). Scanning an unsorted array is O(n). Binary search halves the range each step so it is O(log n). Checking all pairs is O(n^2).

options: O(1), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2)
O(1), O(n), O(log n), O(n^2)
O(n), O(n), O(log n), O(n)
O(1), O(log n), O(log n), O(n^2)

exercises.title: The doubling test
exercises.promptMd: An algorithm takes 1 second on an input of size n. The input size doubles to 2n. Which complexity class would make the new runtime approximately 4 seconds?

hints.text: Ask: which class quadruples when the input doubles?
O(n^2) means work ~ n^2; doubling n gives (2n)^2 = 4n^2.

exercises.explanationMd: O(n^2): work scales as n^2, so (2n)^2 = 4n^2 — quadrupling. O(n) doubles, O(n log n) slightly more than doubles, O(log n) adds a constant.

options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)

exercises.title: Count the operations

hints.text: The inner loop runs n - i - 1 times for each i.
9 + 8 + ... + 1 = 45. In general it is n(n-1)/2.

exercises.explanationMd: The loop counts all pairs (i, j) with i < j: 10 choose 2 = 45. In general this is n(n-1)/2, which is O(n^2) — the exact shape behind every 'check all pairs' algorithm.

exercises.title: Predict the scale-up
exercises.promptMd: An O(n^2) algorithm takes 1 millisecond on an input of size 1,000. Roughly how long will it take on an input of size 10,000, assuming the same machine and no memory effects? Answer in milliseconds.

hints.text: n grew by a factor of 10. Work grows as n^2, so work grows by 10^2 = 100x.

exercises.explanationMd: Quadratic growth means a 10x input increase costs 100x more work: 100 ms. This is the practical muscle of Big O — predicting the future without running it. And it is why O(n^2) endpoints die under traffic spikes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Big O notation is TRUE?
options: O(2n) is a distinct, better class than O(n)
Big O describes the exact runtime of an algorithm on a specific machine
Big O describes how the amount of work grows with the input size, ignoring constants and lower-order terms
An O(n) algorithm is always faster than an O(n^2) algorithm for every input size
questions.explanation: Big O is about growth shape: constants and lower-order terms are dropped by definition, so O(2n) is O(n), and small-input comparisons can still favor worse classes.

questions.prompt: A function does a single pass over an array of size n, then does binary search over the same array. What is the overall complexity?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: Sequential operations add: O(n) + O(log n) = O(n). The linear pass dominates the log term.

questions.prompt: Which code fragment is O(n^2)?
options: for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 2) work();
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) for (int j = i; j < n; ++j) work();
for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) work();
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) work(); for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) work();
questions.explanation: The nested loop over i and j touching the input performs ~n^2/2 operations. Halving loops are O(log n); two sequential loops are O(n); skipping by 2 is still O(n).

questions.prompt: Why can't you answer 'which program is better?' with wall-clock time alone?
options: Because time measurements are always wrong
Because wall-clock time is specific to one input size and one machine, while complexity describes scaling behavior across sizes
Because compilers optimize everything to the same speed
Because Big O is the only thing that matters and constants never matter
questions.explanation: Time gives today's constants on today's machine; complexity gives the growth curve. The O(n^2) program that wins the benchmark on size 100 loses catastrophically at size 1,000,000.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between 'amortized O(1)' (like std::vector push_back) and 'worst-case O(1)'. Why can a real-time system care about this difference?
questions.explanation: Amortized O(1) means the average over a long sequence is constant: most push_backs are one write, but the occasional growth re-copies everything, costing O(n) on that single call. Worst-case O(1) means no single call is ever expensive. A real-time system (audio, flight control) must meet a deadline on every call, so it cannot tolerate the rare O(n) stall — for it, amortized guarantees are not guarantees at all.

concepts.title: Linear Search
concepts.description: Finding an element in unsorted data by scanning — the only option when there is no order to exploit. Coding exercises on vector<int>: first occurrence and counting occurrences.

content.title: The problem it solves
content.content: Finding an element in an array is the most common operation in software — but if the data is *unsorted*, there is exactly one strategy: look at every element. Linear search is not a compromise here; it is the theoretical optimum. Any algorithm that must find a value in an unordered array of n elements may need to inspect all n of them, because the value could be hiding in the very last slot (or absent entirely).

content.title: Mental model
content.content: You are flipping through a deck of cards looking for the ace of spades. You check card by card from the top. If you find it, you stop early — but if it is not there, you only know that after you have turned over every card. A linear scan is exactly this: check element 0, then 1, then 2, ... until you find the match or run out of cards.

content.title: Simple example
Why it works
content.content:
Correctness rests on a simple invariant: after checking index i, we know the target is not in positions 0 through i. So the loop either finds the first match at some index, or — having checked every position — proves the element is absent.

The complexity is exactly what the problem demands: best case 1 comparison (target first), worst case n (target last or absent), average n/2. All of that is O(n) worst case, and no comparison-based algorithm on unsorted data can do better: an adversary can always place the element at the one position you didn't inspect.

content.title: Common mistakes
content.content:
1. **Off-by-one bounds.** `for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i)` reads one element past the end — undefined behavior. The loop bound is `i < n`, or `i <= n - 1` (careful: `n - 1` on an empty vector is a huge unsigned number).

2. **Returning the value instead of the index.** The contract "index of first occurrence, or -1" must match the signature. Returning `arr[i]` loses the position the caller asked for.

3. **Restarting the scan inside the loop.** Moving `i` back to 0 while scanning (e.g. re-searching after each comparison) turns O(n) into O(n^2) or an infinite loop.

4. **Using a range-for when you need the index.** `for (int x : arr)` cannot return the position. Use an indexed loop or maintain your own counter.

5. **Signed/unsigned comparison.** `i < arr.size()` compares int with size_t; cast: `(int)arr.size()`.

content.title: Real-world use
content.content: C's `memchr` and C++'s `std::find` / `std::count` are linear scans, hand-tuned by the standard library vendor with SIMD instructions that check 16 bytes at a time. Linear scans appear in database *table scans* (when no index exists, the engine reads every row), in network packet inspection, and anywhere the data arrives as a stream you can only read once — you cannot binary search a stream because you cannot jump to its middle without storing it. Linear search is also the warm-up pass inside many fancier algorithms, and the fallback inside hash tables when a bucket chain grows.

content.title: When NOT to use it
content.content:
- **The data is sorted** — binary search turns n comparisons into log2(n).
- **Many lookups against the same data** — build a hash map (average O(1) per query) or sort once and binary search forever after. Paying O(n) once is fine; paying O(n) per query is not.
- **Huge data, hot lookup path** — this is exactly why databases create indexes: an index is precomputed order (or hashing) that makes queries fast, because table scans are O(n) per query.
- **Tiny fixed-size collections** — the constant factor of building any index exceeds the scan cost. Scanning 8 elements is unbeatable.

content.title: What you just learned
content.content:
- Linear search checks elements one by one and stops at the first match.
- Worst case is O(n): the target is last or absent — and that is optimal for unsorted data.
- The invariant "positions 0..i contain no match" is what makes the scan correct.
- Return the *index* (or -1), use correct bounds, and cast size_t comparisons.
- Reach for it on unsorted or streamed data, small arrays, or single-shot lookups.

exercises.title: Find the first occurrence
exercises.promptMd: Write `findFirst(arr, target)` that returns the index of the **first** occurrence of `target` in `arr`, or `-1` if it is not present. `arr` is unsorted and may be empty.

hints.text: Use an indexed for loop from 0 to arr.size() - 1 (cast the size to int).
Return `i` the moment `arr[i] == target`; only return -1 after the loop completes without a match.
An empty vector means the loop never runs and you return -1 — no special case needed.

exercises.explanationMd: A single forward scan with early return. The moment a match is found at index i, we return i; the first match is guaranteed because we scan from the front. If the loop exhausts, -1 means absent. Casting size avoids signed/unsigned comparison warnings.

exercises.title: Count the occurrences
exercises.promptMd: Write `countOccurrences(arr, target)` that returns how many times `target` appears in `arr`. The array may be empty, and values may be negative. Count every match — do not stop early.

hints.text: Scan the whole array with a counter that starts at 0.
Increment the counter every time `arr[i] == target`. No early return — every element must be checked.
An empty array must return 0.

exercises.explanationMd: Unlike findFirst there is no early exit: every element must be compared because each one might be another occurrence. This is the full-scan variant of linear search and stays O(n) in all cases.

exercises.title: The worst case of linear search
exercises.promptMd: An unsorted array holds 1,000 elements. In the WORST case, how many elements must a linear search inspect before it can answer 'not found'?

hints.text: The target might be absent — then every element must be checked before you know.
If it were the last element, you inspect all 1,000. If absent, you also inspect all 1,000.

exercises.explanationMd: Both 'found at the last position' and 'absent' require inspecting all 1,000 elements. That is the O(n) worst case — and why unsorted data is fundamentally limited.

options: It depends on the values in the array

exercises.title: Trace the scan

hints.text: Check i = 0: arr[0] = 7, not 2. i = 1: arr[1] = 2.
First occurrence — the scan stops at the first match, not the last.

exercises.explanationMd: The scan checks index 0 (7 != 2), then index 1 (2 == 2) and returns 1 immediately. It never reaches the second 2 at index 3 because 'first occurrence' stops early.

questions.prompt: What is the best case of linear search on an array of size n?
options: O(n) — the scan always visits every element
O(1) — the target is the first element, found on comparison 1
O(log n) — the scan skips half the array each step
O(n/2) is the best case
questions.explanation: If the target is the first element, one comparison finds it: O(1). Best case measures the fewest steps, which is 1 here. Worst and average remain O(n).

questions.prompt: Why is linear search the OPTIMAL strategy for searching unsorted data?
options: Because it uses the least memory of any search algorithm
Because any correct algorithm may need to inspect all n elements to prove absence
Because compilers optimize it to run in O(1)
Because unsorted data can always be searched with binary search
questions.explanation: In the worst case the value is absent or last, and any algorithm must look at every element to be sure. No comparison-based approach can beat inspecting all n elements on unordered input.

questions.prompt: When should you NOT use linear search?
options: When the array is unsorted and small
When you have many repeated lookups against the same large data set
When the data arrives as a stream you can only read once
When you only need to search once
questions.explanation: Repeated lookups amortize the cost of sorting or hashing: sort once (or build a hash map), then each query is O(log n) or O(1). Linear search pays O(n) per query forever.

questions.prompt: What does the contract 'return the index of the first occurrence, or -1' imply about duplicates?
options: It returns the smallest index holding the target
It returns the largest index holding the target
It returns the count of duplicates
It returns the target's value, not its position
questions.explanation: Scanning from index 0 and returning on the first match yields the smallest (first) index. That is why 'first' must be stated — with duplicates, index choice is otherwise ambiguous.

questions.prompt: Explain why an unsorted array of n elements can require n comparisons to confirm a value is absent, and why this makes linear search optimal for that case.
questions.explanation: To prove absence, the algorithm must establish that the value is not at any position — and each position requires a separate comparison. Since the algorithm has no ordering information, it cannot skip positions, so n comparisons are necessary. Any strategy must therefore do at least the work of a linear scan in the worst case, which is exactly what linear search does.

concepts.title: Binary Search
concepts.description: Searching sorted data in O(log n) by halving the candidate range. Coding exercises: exact search and lower_bound-style approximate search on vector<int>.

content.title: The problem it solves
content.content: Linear search over a million records costs up to a million comparisons per query; at a thousand queries per second that is a billion operations per second — a machine all to itself, and it still loses as data grows. Sorted data offers a radically better deal: log2(1,000,000) is about 20. With binary search you can find any element in roughly 20 comparisons, forever, no matter how much bigger the data gets. The problem: you must actually exploit the sortedness, and the habitual 'check every element' loop throws that advantage away.

content.title: Mental model
content.content:
A dictionary. Open the book at the middle. If your word is alphabetically earlier, the entire second half is dead weight — discard it. If later, discard the first half. Repeat on the remaining pages. Every comparison removes half of the search space, so in 20 halvings a million pages shrink to one.

The key insight: an ordered collection lets one comparison answer 'is it here, or which half is it in?' — information an unordered collection can never give.

content.title: Simple example
Why it works
content.content:
The loop maintains an invariant: *if the target exists, it is inside the window `[lo, hi]`*. At `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` we compare `arr[mid]` with the target. If `arr[mid] < target`, every element left of `mid` is also less than the target (that's what sorted means), so the whole left half is eliminated: `lo = mid + 1`. Otherwise we eliminate the right half: `hi = mid - 1`. The window still satisfies the invariant, and it shrinks to at most half its previous size each step.

Because the window halves every iteration, at most `log2(n)` iterations run before the window is empty (not found) or the target sits at `mid`. That is O(log n) — and why the sortedness precondition is not optional: without it, `arr[mid] < target` tells you nothing about the other half, and the algorithm silently returns garbage.

content.title: Common mistakes
content.content:
1. **`(lo + hi) / 2` overflows** for large signed ints (lo + hi can exceed 2^31 - 1). Use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`.

2. **Infinite loops.** With the `lo <= hi` style, the range must move by `mid + 1` / `mid - 1` — never `lo = mid` or `hi = mid`, or the window stops shrinking. (The half-open `[lo, hi)` lower_bound style is different and must not be mixed with this one.)

3. **Running it on unsorted data.** There is no error, no exception — it silently returns a wrong answer. This is the classic 'passes the test, explodes in production' bug.

4. **Duplicates are ambiguous.** 'Index of 5' when 5 appears three times depends on the variant. Exact search may return any occurrence; only `lower_bound`/`upper_bound` give deterministic semantics.

5. **Forgetting the `(int)` cast** on `arr.size()` — `hi = arr.size() - 1` on an empty vector is a huge unsigned number and the loop runs wild.

content.title: Real-world use
content.content: Database index lookups are binary search generalized: a B-tree node is a sorted array, and each node visit compares against a dozen-plus keys at once. `git bisect` finds the first broken commit by binary-searching history. Debuggers bisect large logs; numeric computing uses the bisection method to find roots. C++'s `std::lower_bound`, `std::upper_bound`, and `std::binary_search` implement this everywhere in standard-library code, and CPython's `bisect` module keeps sorted lists fast. Every time you see 'search in a sorted structure', binary search (or its tree variants) is doing the work.

content.title: When NOT to use it
content.content:
- **The data is unsorted** — you must sort first, and sorting costs O(n log n); that only pays off if you then search many times.
- **One lookup on a small array** — a linear scan's constant factor beats the log2(n) math at n < 20.
- **Exact-key lookups** — a hash table is average O(1) and beats binary search in practice for lookups only.
- **Frequent insertions/deletions in the middle** — keeping an array sorted costs O(n) per insert. Use a balanced tree (`std::map`) where the tree does both search and update in O(log n).

content.title: Approximate variants: lower_bound and upper_bound
content.content:
Real code rarely searches for an exact match; it searches for *insertion points*. `lower_bound(x)` returns the first index with `arr[i] >= x`; `upper_bound(x)` returns the first index with `arr[i] > x`. With them you can find the range of all duplicates (`[lower, upper)` — its width is the count), and answer questions like 'which position would keep the array sorted?'

This generalizes to **binary search on the answer**: find the smallest k such that a monotone predicate `f(k)` is true — the pattern behind scheduling problems, 'minimum container size', and numeric optimization, and one of the most useful tricks in systems and competitive programming.

content.title: What you just learned
content.content:
- Binary search needs sorted data and halves the candidate range per comparison: O(log n).
- The invariant 'target is in [lo, hi]' is preserved by moving lo = mid + 1 / hi = mid - 1.
- Compute mid as lo + (hi - lo)/2 to avoid overflow; never let the window stop shrinking.
- Preconditions are load-bearing: on unsorted data binary search silently lies.
- lower_bound/upper_bound give deterministic answers with duplicates and power 'binary search on the answer'.

exercises.title: Binary search, exact match
exercises.promptMd: Write `binarySearch(arr, target)` that returns the index of `target` in the **sorted** array `arr`, or `-1` if absent. The classic halving loop: check the middle, discard the half that cannot contain the target. The array may be empty.

hints.text: Use `int lo = 0; int hi = (int)arr.size() - 1;` and loop while `lo <= hi`.
mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2. If arr[mid] < target, set lo = mid + 1; if arr[mid] > target, set hi = mid - 1.
If you never move past mid (e.g. lo = mid), the loop never terminates. Empty array: hi = -1, loop never runs, return -1.

exercises.explanationMd: Each iteration eliminates half of the remaining range while keeping the invariant 'target is in [lo, hi]'. The loop ends when the window collapses (absent) or mid hits the target. The mid formula avoids overflow, and the (int) cast makes the empty-array case safe (hi = -1, loop skipped).

exercises.title: Lower bound: first element >= target
exercises.promptMd: Write `lowerBound(arr, target)` on a **sorted** array `arr`: return the index of the first element that is **greater than or equal to** `target`. If no such element exists, return `arr.size()`. This is the std::lower_bound semantics and is deterministic even with duplicates. The array may be empty.

hints.text: Use the half-open window [lo, hi) where hi starts at arr.size() and the answer always lives inside the window.
If arr[mid] < target, everything left of mid is too small: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise mid is a valid candidate (or too big): hi = mid.
Loop while lo < hi; return lo. With duplicates, this returns the first >= position; if all elements are less, the window slides to arr.size().

exercises.explanationMd: The half-open window [lo, hi) always contains the answer: everything before lo is < target, and hi is the first index that is >= target (or arr.size()). Because hi = mid keeps valid candidates (never skipping an answer) and lo = mid + 1 discards only elements proven too small, the loop converges with lo == hi — the lower bound. This same shape powers 'binary search on the answer'.

exercises.title: The precondition is load-bearing
exercises.promptMd: A colleague runs the classic binary search on a large array that was NOT sorted. Why is this dangerous, and what can they expect to happen?

hints.text: Binary search's whole correctness argument relies on 'if arr[mid] < target, the left half is all smaller'.
That claim is only true for sorted data.

exercises.explanationMd: On unsorted data, comparing arr[mid] with target tells you nothing about the other half, so binary search can discard the region that actually contains the target. It typically returns a wrong index or -1 with no error at all — silent failure.

options: It will always throw an out-of-range exception
It silently returns a wrong answer, because the halving argument only holds on sorted data
It still works correctly; sorting is just an optimization
It will crash with a segmentation fault

exercises.title: Trace the halving
exercises.promptMd: Trace the exact-search binary search on `arr = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11}` with `target = 9` (use mid = lo + (hi - lo)/2, starting lo = 0, hi = 5). List the mid indices checked, in order, before the search returns index 4.

hints.text: Second mid = 3 + (5-3)/2 = 4. arr[4] = 9 — found.

exercises.explanationMd: mid sequence: 2 (5 < 9, discard left half), then 4 (9 == 9, found). Only 2 comparisons to find the target in 6 elements — log2(6) ~ 3 bounds it.

questions.prompt: Which mid computation is safest for very large arrays?
options: int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
int mid = hi - lo / 2;
int mid = (hi - lo) / 2;
questions.explanation: lo + (hi - lo)/2 avoids overflow because lo + hi never exceeds 2^31 - 1 before halving. (lo + hi)/2 can overflow when both are near the int maximum.

questions.prompt: What happens if binary search runs on an unsorted array?
options: It throws a std::runtime_error
It silently returns a wrong answer, because the halving logic assumes sortedness
It always returns -1
It returns the correct answer but slower
questions.explanation: There is no runtime check for sortedness. The comparison arr[mid] < target only justifies discarding half the range when the array is sorted, so unsorted input yields garbage silently.

questions.prompt: On a sorted array with duplicates {1, 2, 2, 2, 3}, which call deterministically returns 1?
options: binarySearch(arr, 2) — exact search semantics
lowerBound(arr, 2) — first index with arr[i] >= 2
upperBound(arr, 2) — first index with arr[i] > 2
binarySearch(arr, 3)
questions.explanation: lower_bound gives the first position where the value fits: index 1 for 2. Exact search may return any of the three 2 positions; upper_bound returns 4; binarySearch(arr, 3) returns 4.

questions.prompt: How many comparisons does binary search need to find a value in a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements?
options: About 1,000
About 20
Exactly 10
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the range, so the worst case is log2(1,000,000) ~ 20 comparisons. This is the entire point of binary search.

questions.prompt: Explain why sortedness is a strict precondition for binary search: what exactly breaks if the array is unsorted, and why does the algorithm fail silently instead of with an error?
questions.explanation: Binary search works by eliminating half of the range after each comparison: it assumes that if arr[mid] < target then all elements left of mid are also < target, so they cannot contain the target. That implication only holds for sorted data. On unsorted data the eliminated half can actually contain the target, so the search may miss it and terminate with a wrong index or -1. Nothing signals the failure because the algorithm never checks whether its eliminations were valid — garbage in, garbage out, quietly.

concepts.title: Sorting Basics: Selection Sort
concepts.description: Why sorting matters, and the first sort worth implementing by hand: selection sort with its O(n^2) comparisons and O(n) swaps. Coding exercises: ascending and descending selection sort on vector<int>.

lesson.title: Selection Sort: Pick the Smallest Each Time

content.title: The problem it solves
content.content: Sorted data enables everything else: binary search, merging two datasets, deduplication, nearest-neighbor queries, presentable output, and the first steps of dozens of algorithms. Sorting is so fundamental that every language ships one — but to use them wisely you must understand at least one basic sort from the inside, because the invariants, bugs, and complexity reasoning carry over to every sorting algorithm you will ever meet.

content.title: Mental model
content.content: Selection sort is exactly what a tidy person does with scattered cards: scan the whole deck for the smallest card, place it first; scan the rest for the next smallest, place it second; repeat. Each scan gets shorter by one, because the front of the deck is already finished — you never look back at it. The sorted part grows from the left; the unsorted part shrinks from the right.

content.title: Simple example
Why it works
content.content:
The algorithm maintains an invariant: after i outer iterations, the first i positions hold the i smallest elements in sorted order, and every unsorted element is larger than every sorted one. Finding the minimum of the remaining n - i elements and swapping it into position i preserves the invariant; after n - 1 such steps, all n elements are placed.

Two facts make the complexity easy to pin down. It always performs exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons — sorted input, reverse-sorted input, random input: the inner scan never short-circuits. That is O(n^2) comparisons in every case. But it performs at most n swaps — which makes it a favorite where writes are expensive.

content.title: Common mistakes
content.content:
1. **Outer loop runs to n instead of n - 1.** After n - 1 elements are placed, the last one is necessarily in place. Looping to n works (swapping the max with itself) but is a red flag for off-by-one bugs; the scan `j` from `i` to n on the last pass is wasted work.

2. **Swapping inside the inner loop.** If you `swap(arr[i], arr[j])` every time you see a smaller element instead of tracking `minIdx`, you turn O(n) swaps into O(n^2) writes and defeat the algorithm's main virtue.

3. **Never updating `minIdx`.** If you find a smaller element but forget to record its index, the sort silently does nothing or swaps the wrong elements.

4. **Inner loop starting at i - 1 or at 0.** Starting before `i` re-scans the already-sorted prefix — harmless for correctness, wasteful in work, and a sign you don't trust the invariant. Starting at `i` is the correct baseline.

content.title: Real-world use
content.content: Selection sort is too slow for production-sized data, but its idea lives everywhere: k-th smallest selection, partial sorts (sort only the top 10), and the "find the minimum, swap it into place" pattern inside more complex algorithms. Because it never makes more than n swaps, it appears in embedded and storage-constrained systems where writes wear out hardware (flash and EEPROM). And every serious library sorts tiny arrays with simple O(n^2) methods — std::sort switches to insertion sort below ~16 elements — precisely because constants beat asymptotics when n is small.

content.title: When NOT to use it
content.content:
- **Any input larger than a few dozen elements** — O(n^2) comparisons cost real seconds as n grows; use `std::sort` (introsort, O(n log n)).
- **Nearly sorted data** — insertion sort exploits existing order (O(n) on sorted input) while selection sort stubbornly does all n(n-1)/2 comparisons anyway.
- **Stability matters** — selection sort is unstable: the swap can move an equal element across others. Use `std::stable_sort`.
- **Memory is tight and you still need guarantees** — heapsort and in-place quicksort variants sort in place with O(log n) or O(1) extra space; selection sort's extra space is O(1), but its comparison count is what kills it.

content.title: What you just learned
content.content:
- Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it to the front.
- Invariant: after i passes, the first i positions hold the i smallest elements in order.
- Always n(n-1)/2 comparisons (O(n^2) in best, average, and worst case) but at most n swaps.
- Track the minimum's index and swap once — swapping inside the inner loop defeats the design.
- Reach for it only for tiny arrays or when writes are the scarce resource.

exercises.title: Selection sort, ascending
exercises.promptMd: Implement `selectionSort(arr)` that sorts the vector in **ascending** order using selection sort, in place, and returns the sorted vector. Your implementation must scan the unsorted suffix for the minimum, then swap it into position — no std::sort. The vector may be empty.

hints.text: Outer loop: `for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; ++i)`. Inner loop: `for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)`.
Track `minIdx`, starting at i. Update it when `arr[j] < arr[minIdx]`. Swap after the inner loop completes.
An empty or single-element vector needs no swaps — the loops handle it naturally if the bounds are right.

exercises.explanationMd: Each pass finds the minimum of the unsorted suffix arr[i..n-1] and swaps it into position i, extending the sorted prefix by one. The `if (minIdx != i)` guard skips self-swaps. Returning the sorted vector (modified in place) matches the harness's returnType vector<int> / comparator array.

exercises.title: Selection sort, descending
exercises.promptMd: Implement `selectionSortDescending(arr)` that sorts the vector in **descending** order using selection sort, in place, and returns it. Mirror the ascending version: select the *maximum* of the unsorted suffix each pass. Values may be negative; the vector may be empty.

hints.text: Same structure as ascending selection sort, but track the index of the maximum, not the minimum.
Compare with `arr[j] > arr[maxIdx]` to update the max index.
Edge cases: empty and single-element vectors return unchanged.

exercises.explanationMd: The mirror image of ascending selection sort: the invariant becomes 'the first i positions hold the i largest elements'. The comparison flips to `arr[j] > arr[maxIdx]`, and everything else — swap once per pass, bounds, in-place return — is identical.

exercises.title: Comparisons never change
exercises.promptMd: Selection sort on an array of size n always performs exactly how many comparisons? Which of these statements is TRUE?

hints.text: The inner scan runs n - i - 1 times for each outer i, and the inner scan never stops early.

exercises.explanationMd: The inner loop always scans the full suffix — there is no early exit — so comparisons are always (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2, whether the input is sorted, reverse-sorted, or random. That is the O(n^2) worst, average, and best case for comparisons.

options: n(n-1)/2 comparisons in the worst case, fewer when the array is already sorted
n(n-1)/2 comparisons in every case — sorted or not
n comparisons in the best case
n log n comparisons in the average case

exercises.title: One pass by hand
exercises.promptMd: Selection sort runs on `arr = {4, 2, 5, 1, 3}`. After the FIRST outer pass (i = 0) completes, what does the array look like?

hints.text: The first pass finds the minimum of the whole array and swaps it into position 0.
Minimum of {4, 2, 5, 1, 3} is 1, at index 3. It swaps with arr[0]. The rest stay in place.

exercises.explanationMd: The minimum, 1 at index 3, swaps with arr[0] = 4: the array becomes {1, 2, 5, 4, 3}. Only two elements move; the suffix is still unsorted and unchanged in relative order — the sorted prefix has length 1.

questions.prompt: What invariant does selection sort maintain after i outer passes?
options: The last i elements are sorted
The first i positions hold the i smallest elements in sorted order, and the rest are larger than all of them
Every pair of adjacent elements is in order
The entire array is sorted after i passes
questions.explanation: Each pass extends the sorted prefix by one with the smallest remaining element. The prefix is sorted, and every unsorted element is larger than every prefix element.

questions.prompt: What is selection sort's complexity profile?
options: O(n^2) comparisons and O(n^2) swaps in the worst case
O(n^2) comparisons in all cases, at most O(n) swaps
O(n log n) comparisons average, O(n) swaps
O(n) comparisons best case, O(n^2) swaps worst case
questions.explanation: The inner scan always runs to completion: n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of input. But each pass performs at most one swap, so total swaps are at most n.

questions.prompt: Why is selection sort sometimes preferred in write-limited systems (e.g. flash storage)?
options: It does the fewest comparisons of any sort
It never makes more than n swaps, and swaps are the expensive operation
It uses O(n) extra memory which buffers writes
It is stable, which protects against write wear
questions.explanation: Selection sort trades comparisons for swaps: exactly the right trade when moving data costs more than comparing it. Flash cells wear out with writes.

questions.prompt: Which input does selection sort handle with the FEWEST comparisons?
options: Already sorted input
Reverse-sorted input
All inputs require the same number of comparisons
Inputs with many duplicates
questions.explanation: Selection sort never short-circuits: the inner scan always covers the full suffix, so every input — sorted, reverse-sorted, or random — costs exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons.

questions.prompt: Explain why selection sort performs the same number of comparisons on already-sorted input as on reverse-sorted input, and name an O(n^2) sort that does NOT have this weakness (and why).
questions.explanation: Selection sort's inner loop never knows the suffix is already in order — the only way to prove the current element is the minimum is to compare it against everything remaining, so the full n(n-1)/2 comparisons always happen. Insertion sort lacks this weakness: it stops each pass as soon as the new element has found its place, so it does about n comparisons on already-sorted input (O(n)) while still being O(n^2) in the worst case.

concepts.title: Merge Sort
concepts.description: Divide-and-conquer sorting with a guaranteed O(n log n) bound and stability. Coding exercises: the merge step and a recursive merge sort on vector<int>.

content.title: The problem it solves
content.content: At n = 100,000 a quadratic sort does 5 billion comparisons — seconds to minutes. Sorting a million rows, a genome, or a log file demands something that scales: O(n log n). Merge sort delivers it with a guaranteed bound and stability, and its merge step is the same machinery databases use to combine sorted files on disk. It is also the algorithm behind Python's and Java's production sorters, so understanding it means understanding how half the world's data gets ordered.

content.title: Mental model
content.content: Divide and conquer: split the deck in half, sort each half (the same procedure, recursively, until every pile is a single card — trivially sorted), then merge the two sorted piles the way you'd merge two sorted lists with two thumbs: compare the top card of each pile, take the smaller, repeat until both piles are empty. The recursion does the heavy lifting; the merge is where the order actually emerges.

content.title: Simple example
Why it works
content.content:
Correctness is proven by induction: the base case (zero or one element) is trivially sorted. If both halves are sorted, the two-pointer merge produces a sorted whole — at every step, the smaller of the two current elements is the smallest remaining overall, and taking it leaves both piles sorted. The recursion guarantees the halves are sorted, so the merge's output is sorted. Using `L[i] <= R[j]` (not `<`) when taking from the left pile is what makes the sort *stable*: equal elements keep their original order.

The recursion tree is the star of the show: each call splits a range in half, so the tree has `log2(n)` levels, and at every level the total work across all merges is n elements. Total: O(n log n) — guaranteed, for every input, with no worst-case caveats.

content.title: Common mistakes
content.content:
1. **Forgetting to copy the leftovers.** After the two-pointer loop, one pile is always empty — but you must still drain the other. Skipping the leftover loops silently shrinks the result (classic missing-half bug).

2. **Off-by-one splits.** With `mid = left + (right - left) / 2`, the halves are `[left..mid]` and `[mid+1..right]`. Copying `[left..mid+1]` or merging from `mid` instead of `mid+1` corrupts the range boundaries.

3. **Wrong base case.** `if (left >= right) return;` handles both 0 and 1 element ranges. Writing `if (left == right)` only skips single elements and recurses forever on empty ranges.

4. **Allocating a fresh vector in every recursive call.** Allocating in each call multiplies allocation churn by log n levels. Allocate one buffer and pass it down — or copy the two halves per merge as above, but know the cost.

5. **Using `L[i] < R[j]` instead of `<=`** — equal elements get reordered across the piles and the sort stops being stable.

content.title: Real-world use
content.content: Python's `list.sort()` and Java's object sort are TimSort — a hybrid built on merge sort's run-merging. C++'s `std::stable_sort` is a merge sort. External sorting sorts data bigger than RAM by reading chunks, sorting each, and repeatedly merging them — the merge step is identical, only the piles are files. Databases use sort-merge joins, and the "merge two sorted streams" idea powers everything from `diff` tools to log aggregation. When the problem says 'I have sorted streams that must stay sorted', you are doing a merge.

content.title: When NOT to use it
content.content:
- **Small inputs** — insertion sort's constants beat merge sort below roughly 16 elements; that's why std::sort hybridizes. A pure merge sort on tiny arrays wastes the recursion.
- **O(n) extra space is unacceptable** — merge sort's merge buffer costs O(n). For in-place needs, heapsort (O(1) space, same O(n log n) worst case) or quicksort (O(log n) stack space, better constants) win.
- **Recursion is uncomfortable in your environment** — embedded and real-time contexts often forbid unbounded recursion depth; even so, log2(n) depth for merge sort is tiny (~40 frames for a billion elements).
- **You need a fast in-place stable sort** — that's a genuinely hard problem; std::stable_sort itself uses O(n) extra memory. If stability + in-place + speed are all required, reconsider the data structure instead.

content.title: Complexity: why O(n log n)
content.content:
Let `T(n)` be the work for n elements. Splitting and merging costs O(n), and the problem is divided into two halves: `T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n)`. Unfold the recurrence: the recursion tree has `log2(n)` levels (n, then n/2 + n/2, then n/4 x4, ...), and the work on every level sums to exactly n. So `T(n) = n * log2(n)` — hence O(n log n), for every input, with no best-case luck involved.

Space: the merge buffer. With per-call copies, the stack holds buffers summing n + n/2 + n/4 + ... ~ 2n — still O(n). That O(n) space is merge sort's one tax; it buys guaranteed speed and stability.

content.title: What you just learned
content.content:
- Merge sort splits, sorts recursively, and merges two sorted halves with two pointers.
- Correctness by induction: single elements are sorted; merging two sorted piles is trivially correct.
- O(n log n) worst case, guaranteed: log2(n) levels of n work each.
- Use <= in the merge for stability; copy leftovers; split at mid = left + (right-left)/2.
- The merge step is the same operation behind external sorting, stable_sort, and sort-merge joins.

exercises.title: Merge two sorted vectors
exercises.promptMd: Implement `mergeTwoSorted(a, b)`: both inputs are already sorted ascending; return the merged vector, also sorted ascending. Handle empty inputs. This is the merge step of merge sort, isolated so you can perfect it.

hints.text: Two indices, i and j, walk through a and b; compare a[i] vs b[j] and take the smaller into the result.
When one input runs out, the rest of the other input is already sorted — append it wholesale.
Use <= for equal elements so the merge is stable (left pile first). Cast sizes to int for the loop bounds.

exercises.explanationMd: Two pointers always take the smaller current element, which is guaranteed to be the smallest remaining overall because both inputs are sorted. The leftover loops drain whichever pile is non-empty. reserve() avoids reallocation churn; <= keeps equal elements in stable order. This function is the heart of every merge sort.

exercises.title: Recursive merge sort
exercises.promptMd: Implement `mergeSort(arr)` returning the sorted vector. Recursively split the range in half, sort each half, and merge the sorted halves. Use the helper `mergeTwoHalves(arr, left, mid, right)` for the merge. The vector may be empty.

hints.text: Base case: a range with fewer than 2 elements is already sorted — `if (left >= right) return;`.
Split with `mid = left + (right - left) / 2`; recurse on [left..mid] and [mid+1..right], then merge.
In the merge, copy both halves into temp vectors, then two-pointer merge back into arr[left..right], draining leftovers.

exercises.explanationMd: sortRange recurses until ranges are trivial, then merges bottom-up: each merge of size m costs m work and there are log2(n) levels, so the total is O(n log n). The temporary vectors per merge keep the code simple; a production version would reuse one buffer. Using <= in the merge makes the sort stable. Empty input: sortRange is called with left=0, right=-1, immediately returns.

exercises.title: The recursion tree
exercises.promptMd: Merge sort runs on an array of 8 elements. How many levels of recursion does the recursion tree have (counting the level that starts with the full array as level 1), and how much total work is done per level?

hints.text: Each level splits every range in half: 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1.
At every level, each element belongs to exactly one merge.

exercises.explanationMd: Levels: 8, 4, 2, 1 — four levels total (log2(8) + 1). Each level merges all elements exactly once, so work per level is n = 8, giving 4 * 8 = 32 ~ O(n log n).

options: 3 levels, O(n) work per level
4 levels, O(n) work per level, so ~32 unit operations for n = 8
8 levels, O(1) work per level
log2(n) levels but O(n^2) work per level

exercises.title: Trace the merge step
exercises.promptMd: Two sorted halves about to be merged: left half `{1, 4, 6}`, right half `{2, 3, 5}`. In what order are elements taken by the two-pointer merge?

hints.text: Compare the current heads: 1 vs 2. Take 1, advance left. Compare 4 vs 2.
Continue comparing the current heads until both piles are empty.

exercises.explanationMd: Sequence: 1 (vs 2), 2 (4 vs 2), 3 (4 vs 3), 4 (4 vs 5), 5 (6 vs 5), 6 (leftover). Result {1,2,3,4,5,6} — every step takes the smaller current head, which is always the smallest remaining element.

questions.prompt: What is merge sort's time complexity in the WORST case?
options: O(n^2) — the worst case is reverse-sorted input
O(n log n) — guaranteed for every input, with no worst-case caveats
O(n log n) average but O(n^2) worst case
O(n) — merging is linear
questions.explanation: The recursion tree always has log2(n) levels and each level always does n work, so the total is n log n for every input — this is why merge sort is chosen when guarantees matter.

questions.prompt: Why does merge sort use O(n) extra space?
options: Because recursion itself needs O(n) stack per level
Because the merge step needs a buffer to hold the combined halves while writing back in sorted order
Because it keeps a copy of the input for safety
Because comparisons require temporary variables
questions.explanation: Merging two sorted halves requires somewhere to stage the elements — the classic implementation copies both halves into temporary vectors before two-pointer merging back. That buffer is the O(n) space tax.

questions.prompt: What makes merge sort STABLE?
options: It never moves equal elements
The merge takes from the left half first when elements are equal, using <=, so equal elements keep their original order
It sorts in place so nothing can reorder
Stability is impossible for merge sort
questions.explanation: When L[i] and R[j] are equal, taking the left one first preserves original order. That is the <= in the merge comparison — with < instead, equal elements from the right pile jump ahead and the sort becomes unstable.

questions.prompt: When should you AVOID merge sort?
options: When the input is already sorted
When O(n) extra memory is unacceptable
When stability is required
When the input contains negative numbers
questions.explanation: Merge sort's merge buffer is the price of its guarantees. When memory is the constraint, heapsort (in place, same worst case) or quicksort (small stack) are the alternatives. Sorted input is still O(n log n) for merge sort, and negatives are irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Derive merge sort's complexity: write the recurrence, explain what the recursion tree looks like, and why the total work is n log n rather than n^2.
questions.explanation: The recurrence is T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n): two half-size subproblems plus a linear merge. The recursion tree has log2(n) levels, because each level halves the range sizes. On every level, every element participates in exactly one merge, so the total work per level is O(n). Multiplying levels by per-level work gives O(n log n). It is not n^2 because each element is merged only log2(n) times total — unlike selection sort, where each element is compared against nearly everything at every step.
